claim: A 23-colour flow cytometry panel (Panel One) was developed to characterize mesenchymal populations in first trimester placental villous core cells.
source: In order to investigate mesenchymal populations of the placental core a 23-colour flow cytometry panel (Panel One) was developed by starting from a 16-colour panel designed to investigate adipose-derived stromal vascular fraction on a conventional flow cytometer (BD FACS Aria II) (Brooks et al., 2020).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the development of a 23-colour panel and references prior work.

claim: β4 integrin uniquely identifies cytotrophoblasts in the placenta.
source: Cell adhesion molecule that uniquely identifies cytotrophoblasts in the placenta.
evidence: Table 1 states this functional capacity with citation to James et al., 2015.

claim: CD45 is expressed on all nucleated haematopoietic cells.
source: Expressed on all nucleated haematopoietic cells.
evidence: Table 1 provides this information with citation to Hermiston et al., 2003.

claim: HLA-DR is expressed by antigen presenting cells and is involved in antigen presentation and adaptive immunity.
source: Expressed by antigen presenting cells i.e. macrophages, MHC class II cell surface receptor, involved in antigen presentation and adaptive immunity,
evidence: Table 1 describes this functional role with citation to Cruz-Tapias et al., 2013.

claim: CD235a/GPA is a red blood cell marker that identifies early emerging RBCs/erythroblasts from haemogenic endothelium.
source: Red blood cell marker, identifies early emerging RBCs/erythroblasts from haemogenic endothelium
evidence: Table 1 provides this functional description with citations to Garcia-Alegria et al., 2018; Mao et al., 2016.

claim: CD41 is a platelet marker expressed by earliest emerging haematopoietic cells from haemogenic endothelium.
source: Platelet marker. Expressed by earliest emerging haematopoietic cells from haemogenic endothelium
evidence: Table 1 describes this with citations to Garcia-Alegria et al., 2018; Li et al., 2005.

claim: CD117/cKIT is a receptor expressed on haematopoietic stem cells and involved in their differentiation.
source: Receptor expressed on haematopoietic stem cells and involved in their differentiation
evidence: Table 1 provides this functional description with citation to Rönnstrand, 2004.

claim: CD144/VE-cadherin is an endothelial cell-cell adherens junctional marker that stabilises vessels, inhibits vascular growth, and regulates vascular permeability.
source: Endothelial cell-cell adherens junctional marker, stabilises vessels, inhibits vascular growth, regulates vascular permeability.
evidence: Table 1 describes these functions with citation to Giannotta et al., 2013.

claim: CD34 is expressed by haematopoietic and vascular progenitors and adipose-derived MSCs and is thought to identify early placental progenitors.
source: Expressed by haematopoietic and vascular progenitors and adipose-derived MSCs. Transmembrane phosphoglycoprotein, thought to identify early placental progenitors
evidence: Table 1 provides this description with citations to Brooks et al., 2020; Sidney et al., 2014; Yoder, 2009.

claim: CD31/PECAM1 is expressed by endothelial cells, platelets, macrophages and Kupffer cells, granulocytes, lymphocytes, and megakaryocytes.
source: Expressed by endothelial cells, platelets, macrophages and Kupffer cells, granulocytes, lymphocytes, megakaryocytes. Adhesion molecule found at endothelial intercellular junctions.
evidence: Table 1 describes this expression pattern with citation to Marelli-Berg et al., 2013.

claim: VEGFR2/KDR is expressed by endothelial cells and thought to identify placental core progenitors, and is involved in vasculogenesis and angiogenesis.
source: Expressed by endothelial cells and thought to identify placental core progenitors. Receptor for angiogenic VEGF, involved in vasculogenesis and angiogenesis.
evidence: Table 1 provides this functional description with citation to Demir et al., 2007.

claim: CD54/ICAM1 is expressed at low levels on endothelial cells, monocytes and lymphocytes, with increased expression in response to inflammatory cytokines.
source: Expressed at low levels on endothelial cells, monocytes and lymphocytes. Increased expression in response to inflammatory cytokines.
evidence: Table 1 describes this expression pattern with citation to Hubbard and Rothlein, 2000.

claim: CD36/FAT is expressed by microvascular endothelial cells and fibroblasts, has an anti-angiogenic effect via binding Thrombospondin 1, and is involved in fatty acid uptake.
source: Expressed by microvascular endothelial cells, and fibroblasts. Has an anti-angiogenic effect via binding Thrombospondin 1. Involved in fatty acid uptake.
evidence: Table 1 provides these functional descriptions with citations to Dye et al., 2001; Heinzelmann et al., 2018; Silverstein and Febbraio, 2009.

claim: CD90/Thy-1 is expressed by MSCs, haematopoietic stem cells, fibroblasts, and myofibroblasts.
source: Expressed by MSCs, haematopoietic stem cells, fibroblasts, myofibroblasts.
evidence: Table 1 describes this expression pattern with citation to Viswanathan et al., 2019.

claim: CD73/NT5E is expressed by MSCs and endothelial cells and works with CD39 to convert extracellular ATP to adenosine to create immunosuppressive effect.
source: Expressed by MSCs and endothelial cells. Works with CD39 to convert extracellular ATP to adenosine to create immunosuppressive effect.
evidence: Table 1 provides this functional description with citations to Roh et al., 2020; Viswanathan et al., 2019.

claim: CD39/NTPDase is upregulated by MSCs to suppress lymphocyte activation through conversion of extracellular ATP into adenosine.
source: Upregulated by MSCs to suppress lymphocyte activation. Immunosuppressive actions via the conversion of extracellular ATP (inflammatory) into adenosine (anti-inflammatory)
evidence: Table 1 describes this function with citations to Saldanha-Araujo et al., 2011; Zhao et al., 2017.

claim: CD55/DAF is expressed by MSCs and is a complement regulatory protein that inhibits C3 convertases, with increased expression correlated with evasion of innate immune system.
source: Expressed by MSCs. Complement regulatory protein, inhibits C3 convertases thereby creating a threshold for complement activation, increased expression correlated with evasion of innate immune system
evidence: Table 1 provides this description with citations to Ruiz-Argüelles and Llorente, 2007; Soland et al., 2013.

claim: CD271/NGFR/p75NTR is used in MSC and pericyte identification and is hypothesised to identify progenitor populations with superior differentiation and colony forming capacity.
source: Used in MSC and pericyte identification. Hypothesised to identify "stem-cell" or progenitor populations with superior differentiation and colony forming capacity.
evidence: Table 1 describes this with citations to Barilani et al., 2018; Kumar et al., 2017.

claim: CD146/MCAM is an adhesion molecule expressed by pericytes, endothelial cells and smooth muscle cells, involved in the regulation of angiogenesis and vessel permeability.
source: Adhesion molecule expressed by pericytes, endothelial cells and smooth muscle cells. Involved in the regulation of angiogenesis and vessel permeability.
evidence: Table 1 provides this description with citations to Crisan et al., 2009; Leroyer et al., 2019.

claim: CD248 is a pericyte and stromal cell marker involved in cell–cell adhesion and host defence.
source: Pericyte and stromal cell marker. Involved in cell–cell adhesion, and host defence.
evidence: Table 1 describes this with citations to Lax et al., 2010; Tomkowicz et al., 2010.

claim: CD142/TF expression is correlated with pericytes, smooth muscle and fibroblasts, and activates blood clotting after injury.
source: Expression correlated with pericytes, smooth muscle and fibroblasts. Activates blood clotting after injury, located outside the vasculature,
evidence: Table 1 provides this description with citations to Abe et al., 1999; Morrissey, 2004.

claim: CD26/DDP4 is expressed by many tissues including T-cells, epithelial cells, ESCs, progenitor cells, and placental myofibroblasts, and downregulation is correlated with increased stromal/myofibroblast proliferation.
source: Expressed by many tissues; T-cells, epithelial cells, ESCs, progenitor cells, placental myofibroblasts. Serine protease that cleaves a range of chemokines. Downregulation is correlated with increased stromal/myofibroblast proliferation.
evidence: Table 1 provides this description with citations to Kohnen et al., 1996; Mezawa et al., 2019; Ou et al., 2013.

claim: Podoplanin is a lymphatic vascular marker, and its expression is correlated with increased fibroblast migration.
source: Lymphatic vascular marker. Expression is correlated with increased fibroblast migration. Binds to CLEC-2 receptor on platelets.
evidence: Table 1 provides this description with citations to Astarita et al., 2012; Suchanski et al., 2017.

claim: β4 integrin localizes to cytotrophoblasts in placental villus sections.
source: localisation of (C) β4 integrin (red) to cytotrophoblasts
evidence: Figure 1C shows immunofluorescence localization of β4 integrin to cytotrophoblasts.

claim: CD144 and CD31 localize to blood vessels in placental villus sections.
source: (E) CD144 (red) and CD31 (green) to blood vessels (white arrows) in placental villus sections confirmed antibody specificity.
evidence: Figure 1E shows immunofluorescence localization of CD144 and CD31 to blood vessels.

claim: Five distinct subsets were uncovered in the villous core using viSNE clustering combined with known population marker expression.
source: Combining viSNE with known population marker expression, five distinct subsets were uncovered (Figure 2).
evidence: The manuscript states that five subsets were identified using viSNE analysis.

claim: Endothelial cells (Subset One) co-expressed CD31 and CD34 and made up 3.9% ± 2.5% of villous core cells.
source: Endothelial cells co-expressed CD31 and CD34 (Subset One) and made up 3.9% ± 2.5% of villous core cells (Figure 3C and D).
evidence: The manuscript provides quantitative data on the percentage of endothelial cells.

claim: CD73+CD90+ mesenchymal cells (Subset Two) made up 6.8% ± 9.7% of villous core cells on average.
source: CD73+CD90+ mesenchymal cells (Subset Two) made up 6.8% ± 9.7% of villous core cells on average
evidence: The manuscript provides quantitative data on the percentage of CD73+CD90+ cells.

claim: CD73+CD90+ cells decreased in abundance with increasing gestational age within the first trimester.
source: CD73+CD90+ mesenchymal cells (Subset Two) made up 6.8% ± 9.7% of villous core cells on average, but decreased in abundance with increasing gestational age within the first trimester (Figure 2C).
evidence: The manuscript states this observation and references Figure 2C.

claim: At <10 weeks of gestation CD73+CD90+ cells constituted 14.02+8.84% of villous core cells, but significantly decreased to 0.77+0.83% at ≥10 weeks of gestation (P<0.001, n=27).
source: Together this data showed that at <10 weeks of gestation CD73+CD90+ cells constituted 14.02+8.84% of villous core cells, but significantly decreased to 0.77+0.83% of villous core cells at ≥10 weeks of gestation (P<0.001, n=27, placentae = 7–13.1 weeks of gestation) (Figure 3C).
evidence: The manuscript provides quantitative data with statistical significance.

claim: Perivascular cells (Subset Three) were identified by their expression of CD146+CD271+ and constituted 10.3% ± 4.7% of villous core cells.
source: Perivascular cells (Subset Three) were identified by their expression of CD146+CD271+, and constituted 10.3% ± 4.7% of villous core cells (Figure 3C).
evidence: The manuscript provides quantitative data on the percentage of perivascular cells.

claim: Subset Four made up the largest proportion of mesenchymal cells in the core (47.8+17.0%) and were identified by co-expression of podoplanin+CD36+.
source: Subset Four made up the largest proportion of mesenchymal cells in the core (47.8+17.0%) and were identified by co-expression of podoplanin+CD36+ (Figure 3C).
evidence: The manuscript provides quantitative data on the percentage of podoplanin+CD36+ cells.

claim: Subset Five, expressing CD26+CD90+, constituted 31.3% ± 12.6% of villous core cells and were classified as myofibroblast-like cells.
source: The remaining cells, expressing only the myofibroblast-associated markers CD26+CD90+, were classified as Subset Five and constituted 31.3% ± 12.6% of villous core cells. Subset Five were negative for all other markers investigated, suggesting they are more differentiated myofibroblast-like cells (Figure 3C).
evidence: The manuscript provides quantitative data and interpretation of the phenotype.

claim: CD73+CD90+ cells (Subset Two) were the only villous population to co-express CD90 and CD73.
source: CD73+CD90+ cells (Subset Two) were the only villous population to co-express CD90 and CD73, both MSC-associated markers.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this unique co-expression pattern.

claim: CD73+CD90+ cells also expressed podoplanin, low levels of CD142, and had heterogeneous expression of CD146 and CD271.
source: This subset also expressed podoplanin (correlated with increased migratory capacity), low levels of CD142 (involved in blood coagulation [Morrissey, 2004]), and had heterogeneous expression of CD146 and CD271 (perivascular associated markers) (Figure 3B).
evidence: The manuscript describes the expression pattern with reference to Figure 3B.

claim: CD73+CD90+ cells lacked CD26 expression, making them distinct from other perivascular and mesenchymal cell populations.
source: A lack of CD26 (associated with myofibroblasts and cell proliferation) made this population distinct from the other perivascular and mesenchymal cell populations identified in the villous core using Panel One.
evidence: The manuscript states this distinguishing feature.

claim: Perivascular cells (Subset Three) did not co-express CD73, CD142 or podoplanin.
source: Perivascular cells (Subset Three), identified by expression of CD271 or CD146, did not co-express CD73, CD142 or podoplanin.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the lack of these markers.

claim: Perivascular cells expressed CD26 and CD90 and co-localised with Subset Five on the viSNE plot.
source: However, they did express CD26 and CD90, and in line with this they co-localised with Subset Five (also CD26+CD90+) on the viSNE plot (Figure 3B).
evidence: The manuscript describes marker expression and spatial relationship on viSNE plot.

claim: Subset Four co-expressed CD26, CD90, and CD142, but was negative for CD73.
source: Subset Four was identified by expression of podoplanin and CD36, and co-expressed CD26, CD90, and CD142, but was negative for the MSC-associated marker CD73 (Figure 3B).
evidence: The manuscript describes the marker expression pattern.

claim: Subset Four was considered the most likely in vivo candidate to contribute to pMSCs derived in explant cultures due to being the largest population and expressing proliferative/migratory markers.
source: As the largest population within the villous core and expressing proliferative/migratory associated markers (CD26, podoplanin [Suchanski et al., 2017]) this subset was considered the most likely in vivo candidate to contribute to pMSCs that are derived in explant derived cultures.
evidence: The manuscript provides reasoning based on population size and marker expression.

claim: Both CD73+CD90+ cells and podoplanin+CD36+ cells underwent phenotypic convergence in culture, forming cells with mesenchymal-like morphology that were CD90+CD73+CD142+CD271-CD36- at day 7.
source: In culture, both populations underwent phenotypic convergence, forming cells with a mesenchymal-like morphology, that were CD90+CD73+CD142+CD271-CD36- at day 7 of culture (Figure 4B and C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript describes the phenotypic changes observed after culture.

claim: CD26 was only expressed by a small proportion of CD73+CD90+ cells at isolation and although the percentage increased over time in culture, most cells remained negative.
source: The proliferation/myofibroblast associated marker CD26 was only expressed by a small proportion of CD73+CD90+ cells at the time of isolation and although the percentage of CD26+ cells increased over time in culture, most cells remained negative suggesting this marker was not upregulated with the culture conditions used here.
evidence: The manuscript describes the CD26 expression pattern in CD73+CD90+ cells over time.

claim: All podoplanin+CD36+ cells were CD26+ at isolation and remained CD26+ after culture.
source: Conversely, all podoplanin+CD36+ cells were CD26+ at isolation and remained CD26+ after culture.
evidence: The manuscript describes the stable CD26 expression in podoplanin+CD36+ cells.

claim: A subpopulation of CD73+CD90+ cells expressed CD146 (5.89+5.82%) at day 0, whereas podoplanin+CD36+ cells were negative for CD146.
source: Although CD146, was used to identify perivascular cells in the placenta (Castrechini et al., 2010), was not assessed on cells during isolation (this marker was not contained in Panel Two), phenotyping experiments with Panel One demonstrated that a subpopulation of CD73+CD90+ cells expressed CD146 (5.89+5.82%) and therefore, could be perivascular. Whereas, podoplanin+CD36+ cells were negative for CD146.
evidence: The manuscript provides quantitative data on CD146 expression.

claim: After 7 days culture, the CD146+ subpopulation was still present in CD73+CD90+ cells (15.55+6.87%), but all podoplanin+CD36+ cells expressed CD146.
source: After 7 days culture this CD146+ subpopulation was still present in CD73+CD90+ cells (15.55+6.87%). However, all podoplanin+CD36+ cells expressed CD146 after seven days in culture, demonstrating differential response of these subsets to the in vitro culture conditions (Figure 4D and E, and Figure 4—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: The manuscript provides quantitative data showing differential CD146 expression changes.

claim: Explant isolated pMSCs were CD90low/negCD73+CD26+CD142+CD146+podo+CD34-CD271-CD36-.
source: This demonstrated that pMSCs were CD90low/negCD73+CD26+CD142+CD146+podo+CD34-CD271-CD36-(Figure 4F and Figure 4—figure supplements 1 and 2)
evidence: The manuscript provides the phenotypic characterization of pMSCs.

claim: The phenotype of explant isolated pMSCs more closely aligned with cultured podoplanin+CD36+ cells (Subset Four) rather than CD73+CD90+ cells (Subset Two).
source: This demonstrated that pMSCs were CD90low/negCD73+CD26+CD142+CD146+podo+CD34-CD271-CD36-(Figure 4F and Figure 4—figure supplements 1 and 2), more closely aligning with the phenotype of cultured podoplanin+CD36+ cells (Subset Four).
evidence: The manuscript compares phenotypes and draws this conclusion.

claim: pMSCs upregulate the contractile markers αSMA and calponin when transferred from EGM-2 to standard MSC medium (advanced-DMEM/F12).
source: In previous work we have demonstrated that pMSCs upregulate the contractile markers αSMA and calponin when transferred from EGM-2 to standard MSC medium (advanced-DMEM/F12) (Boss et al., 2020).
evidence: The manuscript cites prior work demonstrating this phenomenon.

claim: Both CD73+CD90+ cells and podoplanin+CD36+ cells upregulated αSMA and calponin when transferred from EGM-2 to advanced-DMEM/F12.
source: Whilst in EGM-2 very few cells in either population expressed αSMA and no cells expressed calponin, in advanced-DMEM/F12, both populations upregulated both of these markers (Figure 5).
evidence: The manuscript describes the experimental results shown in Figure 5.

claim: Expression of the more mature smooth muscle marker MYH-11 was not observed in either CD73+CD90+ or podoplanin+CD36+ cells cultured in either EGM-2 or advanced DMEM/F12.
source: Expression of the more mature smooth muscle marker MYH-11 was not observed in either CD73+CD90+ or podoplanin+CD36+ cells cultured in either EGM-2 or advanced DMEM/F12 (Figure 5).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the absence of MYH-11 expression.

claim: MSCs from different tissue sources functionally differ in a tissue-specific manner despite sharing expression of minimal criteria antigens after in vitro culture.
source: However, despite MSCs from different tissue sources (i.e. bone-marrow, adipose, umbilical cord, placenta) sharing expression of the minimal criteria antigens after in vitro culture, they functionally differ in a tissue-specific manner (Du et al., 2016b; Kozlowska et al., 2019).
evidence: The manuscript cites literature supporting this claim.

claim: In vitro culture may have significant impact on MSC phenotype, meaning that cultured MSCs may have a different phenotype from their in vivo/freshly isolated counterparts.
source: It has become clear that in vitro culture may have significant impact on MSC phenotype, meaning that cultured MSCs may have a different phenotype from their in vivo/freshly isolated counterparts.
evidence: The manuscript states this as an established understanding in the field.

claim: Prior to culture adipose-derived MSCs are CD34+, whilst in vitro culture induces the loss of CD34 expression.
source: For example, prior to culture adipose-derived MSCs are CD34+, whilst in vitro culture induces the loss of CD34 expression (Lin et al., 2012).
evidence: The manuscript cites literature demonstrating this culture-induced change.

claim: The MSC-associated marker CD271 is lost with plastic culture.
source: The MSC-associated marker CD271 is also lost with plastic culture (Brooks et al., 2020)
evidence: The manuscript cites literature demonstrating this culture-induced change.

claim: MSC αSMA expression can be heavily impacted by culture media.
source: and MSC αSMA expression can be heavily impacted by culture media (Boss et al., 2020).
evidence: The manuscript cites literature demonstrating this culture-induced change.

claim: pMSCs have been reported to reside in a perivascular niche where they can influence vascular development and function.
source: pMSCs have been reported to reside in a perivascular niche where they can influence vascular development and function (Castrechini et al., 2010).
evidence: The manuscript cites literature reporting this localization.

claim: Cultured pMSCs have well established angiogenic and haematopoietic paracrine effects in vitro and in vivo.
source: In line with this, cultured pMSCs have well established angiogenic and haematopoietic paracrine effects in vitro and in vivo (Chen et al., 2009; Du et al., 2016a).
evidence: The manuscript cites literature supporting these functional properties.

claim: Work with bone marrow MSCs suggest CD146 expression is a tissue culture artefact.
source: However, work with bone marrow MSCs suggest CD146 expression is a tissue culture artefact (Blocki et al., 2013)
evidence: The manuscript cites literature suggesting CD146 is culture-induced.

claim: Chipcytometry has localised in vitro MSC markers CD73, CD105 and CD90 outside of the perivascular niche in term placentae.
source: and chipcytometry has localised in vitro MSC markers CD73, CD105 and CD90 outside of the perivascular niche in term placentae (Consentius et al., 2018).
evidence: The manuscript cites literature demonstrating this localization.

claim: Bone marrow MSCs isolated by their expression of CD146 stabilize endothelial tube formation in vitro, whereas CD146- MSCs that subsequently upregulate CD146 in vitro are unable to stabilize tube formation.
source: For example bone-marrow MSCs isolated by their expression of CD146 stabilize endothelial tube formation in vitro, whereas, CD146- MSCs, that subsequently upregulate CD146 in vitro, are unable to stablise tube formation (Blocki et al., 2013).
evidence: The manuscript cites literature demonstrating functional differences based on CD146 expression origin.

claim: The four mesenchymal populations identified closely aligned with populations described in prior single-cell RNA sequencing data from first trimester placentae, except for CD73+CD90+ cells.
source: From the four mesenchymal populations classified in this work three populations, perivascular cells (Subset Three), podoplanin+CD36+ cells (Subset Four), and CD26+CD90+ myofibroblasts (Subset Five) all closely aligned with populations described in prior single-cell RNA sequencing data from first trimester placentae (Suryawanshi et al., 2018). However, this single-cell RNA sequencing dataset did not report a population that aligned with CD73+CD90+ cells (Subset Two)
evidence: The manuscript compares findings to prior RNA-seq data.

claim: The single-cell RNA sequencing dataset reported that only endothelial cells expressed CD73 in the placental core.
source: instead reporting that only endothelial cells expressed CD73 in the placental core.
evidence: The manuscript describes what was reported in prior RNA-seq work.

claim: The decline in abundance of CD73+CD90+ cells after 9 weeks of gestation corresponds to the regression of villi and blood vessels from the distal side of the gestational sac.
source: As the decline in abundance of these cells after 9 weeks of gestation corresponds to the regression of villi and blood vessels from the distal side of the gestational sac (Burton and Jauniaux, 2018)
evidence: The manuscript correlates the timing of cell decline with known developmental events.

claim: Expression of podoplanin and low expression of CD26 are both associated with a migratory/invasive phenotype.
source: First, expression of podoplanin and low expression of CD26 are both associated with a migratory/invasive phenotype (Mezawa et al., 2019; Ward et al., 2019).
evidence: The manuscript cites literature linking these markers to migration/invasion.

claim: Inhibiting CD26 enhances homing, engraftment and differentiation of hematopoietic stem cells.
source: Several studies have demonstrated that inhibiting CD26 enhances homing, engraftment and differentiation of hematopoietic stem cells (Christopherson et al., 2004; Kawai et al., 2007)
evidence: The manuscript cites literature supporting this functional role of CD26.

claim: Podoplanin identifies connective stroma in lymphoid organs that produces a network of collagen-rich fibres to enable movement of lymphocytes via interactions with leukocyte CLEC-2 receptors.
source: Furthermore, podoplanin identifies connective stroma in lymphoid organs that produces a network of collagen-rich fibres to enable movement of lymphocytes via interactions with leukocyte CLEC-2 receptors (Link et al., 2011; Nazari et al., 2016; Onak Kandemir et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2011).
evidence: The manuscript cites literature describing this function of podoplanin.

claim: Hofbauer cells have been co-localised with podoplanin expressing stroma in term placentae.
source: Indeed, Hofbauer cells have been co-localised with podoplanin expressing stroma in term placentae (Onak Kandemir et al., 2019).
evidence: The manuscript cites literature demonstrating this co-localization.

claim: CD26 identifies fibroblasts involved in wound healing/fibrosis and the associated extracellular matrix deposition.
source: However, podoplanin+CD36+ cells had a high expression of CD26 which identifies fibroblasts involved in wound healing/fibrosis and the associated extracellular matrix deposition (Soare et al., 2020; Worthen et al., 2020)
evidence: The manuscript cites literature linking CD26 to these functions.

claim: The corresponding podoplanin+CD36+ population in prior single cell RNA-seq data expressed genes associated with angiogenesis (IL6, ANGPTL-4, TNFAIP6).
source: The corresponding podoplanin+CD36+ population observed in the prior single cell RNA-seq dataset, expressed genes associated with angiogenesis (IL6, ANGPTL-4, TNFAIP6), suggesting they may also provide a paracrine stimulus for placental vascular development which is undergoing vasculogenesis and angiogenesis over first trimester (Chang et al., 2012; Hato et al., 2008; Suryawanshi et al., 2018).
evidence: The manuscript cites RNA-seq data and literature to support this functional inference.

claim: Prior single-cell RNA sequencing work identified that populations aligning with perivascular cells and CD26+CD90+ myofibroblasts had respectively low or high expression of contractile markers ACTA2 (αSMA) and CNN1 (calponin).
source: Indeed, prior single-cell RNA sequencing work identified that populations aligning with perivascular cells and CD26+CD90+ myofibroblasts reported here had a respectively low or high expression of markers associated with contractile myofibroblasts and mature perivascular cells (ACTA2 (αSMA) and CNN1 (calponin)) (Kumar et al., 2017; Suryawanshi et al., 2018).
evidence: The manuscript cites RNA-seq data supporting this expression pattern.

claim: The first trimester placental vasculature is relatively immature, so perivascular cells would not necessarily be expected to have high expression of contractile markers at this stage of gestation.
source: The lower expression of contractile markers in perivascular cells in comparison to CD26+CD90+ myofibroblasts may initially appear unexpected, but as the first trimester placental vasculature is relatively immature it would not necessarily be expected that perivascular cells had high expression of contractile markers at this stage of gestation (Zhang et al., 2002).
evidence: The manuscript provides reasoning based on developmental stage with citation.

claim: In term placentae contractile perivascular cells express both αSMA and calponin, but extravascular αSMA+ cells are also present and thought to allow stem villi to contract and expand in volume.
source: Indeed, in term placentae contractile perivascular cells express both αSMA and calponin, but extravascular αSMA+ cells are also present and thought to allow stem villi to contract and expand in volume (Dellschaft et al., 2020; Farley et al., 2004).
evidence: The manuscript cites literature describing contractile cell populations in term placenta.

claim: CD73 is thought to be ubiquitously expressed by MSCs.
source: In the MSC field, CD73 is thought to be ubiquitously expressed by MSCs (Dominici et al., 2006).
evidence: The manuscript cites the ISCT criteria for MSCs.

claim: Podoplanin+CD36+ cells upregulate CD73 expression after culture, demonstrating expression of this marker may be a culture artefact.
source: However, that podoplanin+CD36+ cells upregulate CD73 expression after culture demonstrates expression of this marker may also be a culture artefact.
evidence: The manuscript draws this conclusion from the experimental data.

claim: Emerging data has suggested that MSC function is altered in the pregnancy complication fetal growth restriction, with potential impacts on placental vascular function.
source: Indeed, in the context of pregnancy, emerging data has suggested that MSC function is altered in the pregnancy complication fetal growth restriction, with potential impacts on placental vascular function (Boss et al., 2021; Gillmore et al., 2022).
evidence: The manuscript cites recent literature on MSC dysfunction in pregnancy complications.

claim: The initial enzymatic digestion removed the outer syncytiotrophoblast layer.
source: Whilst the initial enzymatic digestion removed the outer syncytiotrophoblast layer, inclusion of the cytotrophoblast maker β4 integrin in Panel One ensured any potential contaminating cytotrophoblasts directly beneath this were also excluded from analysis (Table 1, Figure 1B and C).
evidence: The manuscript describes the digestion protocol and its effects.

claim: A mean of 0.95% ± 0.91% of the total live cells were HLAG+ extravillous trophoblasts.
source: A mean of 0.95% ± 0.91% of the total live cells were HLAG + extravillous trophoblasts (Figure 7), and are thus unlikely to impact on downstream stromal analyses.
evidence: The manuscript provides quantitative data on extravillous trophoblast contamination.

claim: Spectral flow cytometry can measure a larger portion of the spectral signature of each fluorophore and enable small differences between fluorophores to be discriminated.
source: The ability of spectral flow cytometry to measure a larger portion of the spectral signature of each fluorophore, and thus enable small differences between fluorophores to be discriminated, combined with the ability to remove autofluorescence (a prominent feature of mesenchymal cells) paves the way for assessing cells previously regarded as challenging for multicolour flow cytometry.
evidence: The manuscript describes the technical advantages of spectral flow cytometry.

claim: The largest multicolour panel used to assess mesenchymal cells to date was 16-colours and was designed for analysis with conventional flow cytometry.
source: To date the largest panel used to assess mesenchymal cells (16-colours) was designed for analysis with conventional flow cytometry (Brooks et al., 2020).
evidence: The manuscript cites prior work establishing the previous state of the art.

claim: This work developed what to the authors' knowledge is the largest multicolour spectral flow cytometry panel employed to date.
source: Here, we developed what to our knowledge is the largest multicolour spectral flow cytometry panel employed to date, in order to characterise the mesenchymal heterogeneity in first trimester placental tissue, and to ascertain the impact of in vitro MSC culture conditions on the subsequent phenotype of these populations.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly claims this achievement.

claim: CD73+CD90+ cells may represent a functionally divergent population that is abundant in the early first trimester placenta which is specialised to facilitate/promote hematopoietic migration and differentiation, and morphogenesis of the placenta during regression of the distal villi.
source: Together this suggests CD73+CD90+ cells may represent a functionally divergent population, that is abundant in the early first trimester placenta which is specialised to facilitate/promote hematopoietic migration and differentiation, and morphogenesis of the placenta during regression of the distal villi.
evidence: The manuscript proposes this functional interpretation based on marker expression and timing.

claim: Podoplanin+CD36+ cells may play a role in facilitating hematopoietic transport throughout the poorly vascularised first trimester stroma and may have a migratory phenotype.
source: Similar to CD73+CD90+ cells, the expression of podoplanin in this population suggests they may play a role in facilitating hematopoietic transport throughout the poorly vascularised first trimester stroma, and may have a migratory phenotype.
evidence: The manuscript proposes this functional role based on marker expression.

claim: The in vivo niche that CD73+CD90+ cells and podoplanin+CD36+ cells reside in could determine whether differentiated cells contribute to perivascular or myofibroblast contractile cells.
source: The in vivo niche that CD73+CD90+ cells and podoplanin+CD36+ cells reside in could determine whether differentiated cells contribute to perivascular or myofibroblast contractile cells and more specific markers may be required to tease apart these differences.
evidence: The manuscript proposes this hypothesis about niche-dependent differentiation.

claim: Ex vivo phenotype may be a more accurate indicator of a cells' functional capacity than cultured phenotype.
source: Thus, ex vivo phenotype may be a more accurate indicator of a cells' functional capacity and highlights the importance of characterizing mesenchymal cells prior to culture.
evidence: The manuscript draws this conclusion from the discussion of culture-induced changes.

claim: The population/s with a competitive advantage in culture are likely to outcompete and become the dominant cell in culture.
source: However, the population/s with a competitive advantage in culture, either as a result of the culture conditions employed, or as a result of the isolation process itself (enzymes involved, explant-based, plated suspension, enriched for expression of a marker), are likely to outcompete and become the dominant cell in culture.
evidence: The manuscript proposes this mechanism for culture selection.

claim: Under different media conditions fetal pMSCs rather than maternal cells are enriched in culture in EGM-2.
source: Indeed, our group has demonstrated that under different media conditions fetal pMSCs rather than maternal cells are enriched in culture in EGM-2 (Boss et al., 2020).
evidence: The manuscript cites prior work demonstrating media-dependent selection.

claim: The heterogeneity identified creates an opportunity to select subsets of mesenchymal cells more suited to specific uses with anti-inflammatory/immunomodulatory or angiogenic capacity.
source: The heterogeneity identified in this work creates an opportunity to select subsets of these mesenchymal cells more suited to specific uses i.e. with anti-inflammatory/immunomodulatory or angiogenic capacity, and to target media conditions that maintain or transform their in vivo phenotype and desired properties.
evidence: The manuscript proposes this application of the findings.

claim: CD142 expression on Subset Four may have a potential pro-coagulant role that is a limitation for therapeutic applications.
source: Finally, it is important to consider potential limitations of the use of the cell types identified in therapeutic applications, for example the potential pro-coagulant role of cell surface expression of CD142 (Subset Four) (Moll et al., 2020)
evidence: The manuscript discusses potential therapeutic limitations with citation.

claim: CD36 expression on Subset Four may indicate these cells could be prone to differentiating down the adipose pathway in vivo.
source: or the prior association of CD36 expression (seen on Subset Four) with adipose progenitors, raising the possibility that these cells could be prone to differentiating down this pathway in vivo (Gao et al., 2017; Hanschkow et al., 2022).
evidence: The manuscript discusses potential differentiation propensity with citations.

claim: Expression of podoplanin may indicate an increased migratory capacity, which could potentially enhance migration to sites of therapeutic interest when administered in vivo.
source: Conversely, the expression of podoplanin (Subset Two and Four), may indicate an increased migratory capacity, which could potentially enhance migration to sites of therapeutic interest when administered in vivo (Ward et al., 2019).
evidence: The manuscript proposes this potential therapeutic advantage with citation.
